newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korea to close contact point with South.
newsitem.headline: North Korea to close contact point with South.

text.p: North Korea said on Tuesday it would temporarily abandon a border liaison office set up in 1992 as a gesture of reconciliation during a rare blossoming of goodwill between the rival Koreas.
The move indicated a further deterioration of relations that have turned icy following the incursion of a North Korean submarine in September.
A communique issued by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said the action was in response to remarks by South Korean President Kim Young-sam shutting the door to dialogue.

The office in the border hamlet of Panmunjom was established to promote civilian contacts, including cultural and government exchanges, and to facilitate family reunions after the prime ministers of North and South Korea signed a non-aggression treaty in 1991.
Panmunjom is the only crossing point on the Demilitarized Zone that sealed the division of the Korean peninsula following the 1950-53 Korean War.

The liaison office was opened as a separate channel of communication to the Military Armistice Commission, which monitors a ceasefire that ended the war and holds regular meetings in a conference room that straddles the Korean border.
The KCNA statement said North Korean delegates to the liaison office "will tentatively withdraw and suspend their business there from November 20".
It said that in a November 9 interview with the Washington Post newspaper Kim had ruled out dialogue with the North.
"Now that the chief executive of South Korea has adopted a totally negative attitude toward dialogue, the term of dialogue has become meaningless in Korea," the statement said.
"Accordingly, the existence of the Panmunjom liaison office, which is in charge of liaison and technical consultation for inter-Korean dialogue, has become meaningless," it added.
South Korea urged Pyongyang to reconsider, even though it has frozen all contacts with the North until Pyongyang apologises for the submarine intrusion.
"The South Korean government strongly urges North Korea to withdraw such an unreasonable action and normalise the liaison office," a Unification Ministry statement said.
South Korea was embarrassed and frightened by the infiltration of the submarine that landed 26 North Koreans on a Southern beach.

Twenty-four of the crew have been shot and killed, one captured alive and another is on the run. Pyongyang maintains the whole incident was an accident and is demanding the return of the bodies and the captured agent.
Seoul-based Western diplomats said the closure of the liaison office would have little practical effect, and the North Korean move was largely symbolic.
"I would interpret this as a very low cost way to express disapproval," said one envoy.
Nevertheless, closing the office adds to tension on the last Cold War-era frontier.

Last year, North Korea said it was abandoning its obligations under the armistice agreement that ended the Korean War and repeatedly sent heavily armed troops into the Demilitarized Zone in violation of the accord.
On Tuesday, a Military Armistice commission meeting was held in Panmunjom to discuss Pyongyang's demands for the return of the submarine crew.

Representatives of the U.S.-led United Nations Command that represents South Korea at the commission told Northern military officers the matter should be resolved between North and South Korea, a U.N. Command statement said.
